title: Wise flight, and the women who provided
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ μὴ προπετεῖς εἶναι διδάσκων τοὺς μαθητὰς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς τό· „ἐὰν διώκωσιν ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ, φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἑτέραν· κἂν ἐν τῇ ἑτέρᾳ διώκωσι, πάλιν φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἄλλην,“ καὶ διδάσκων παράδειγμα αὐτοῖς ἐγίνετο εὐσταθοῦς βίου, οἰκονομοῦντος μὴ εἰκῆ μηδ᾿ ἀκαίρως καὶ ἀλόγως ὁμόσε χωρεῖν τοῖς κινδύνοις· τοῦτο πάλιν κακουργῶν ὁ Κέλσος διαβάλλει, καί φησι πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὁ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ Ἰουδαῖος ὅτι μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν τῇδε κἀκεῖσε ἀποδιδράσκεις. ὅμοιον δὲ ᾗ πεποίηται κατὰ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν διαβολῇ φήσομεν εἶναι καὶ τὸ περὶ Ἀριστοτέλους ἱστορούμενον· οὗτος γὰρ ἰδὼν συγκροτεῖσθαι μέλλον κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ δικαστήριον ὡς κατὰ ἀσεβοῦς διά τινα δόγματα τῆς φιλοσοφίας αὐτοῦ, ἃ ἐνόμισαν εἶναι ἀσεβῆ Ἀθηναῖοι, ἀναχωρήσας ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν ἐν Χαλκίδι τὰς διατριβὰς ἐποιήσατο, ἀπολογησάμενος τοῖς γνωρίμοις καὶ λέγων· „ἀπίωμεν ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν, ἵνα μὴ πρόφασιν δῶμεν Ἀθηναίοις τοῦ δεύτερον ἄγος ἀναλαβεῖν παραπλήσιον τῷ κατὰ Σωκράτους, καὶ ἵνα μὴ δεύτερον εἰς φιλοσοφίαν ἀσεβήσωσι.“ φησὶ δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αἰσχρῶς καὶ γλίσχρως τὰς τροφὰς συλλέγοντα περιεληλυθέναι. πόθεν λαβὼν, ἀπαγγελλέτω, τὸ αἰσχρὸν καὶ τὸ γλίσχρον τῆς συλλογῆς· ἐν γὰρ τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις „γυναῖκές τινες,“ „τεθεραπευμέναι ἀπὸ“ τῶν „ἀσθενειῶν“ αὐτῶν, ἐν αἷς ἦν καὶ „Σουσάννα“, παρεῖχον τοῖς μαθηταῖς „ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς“ τροφάς. τίς δὲ τῶν φιλοσοφούντων καὶ ἀνακειμένων ὠφελίᾳ γνωρίμων οὐκ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐλάμβανε τὰ πρὸς τὰς χρείας; ἢ ἐκεῖνοι μὲν τοῦτο καθηκόντως ἐποίουν καὶ καλῶς, ἐπὰν δ᾿ οἱ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ πράττωσιν αὐτὸ, κατηγοροῦνται ὑπὸ Κέλσου ὡς αἰσχρῶς καὶ γλίσχρως συλλέγοντες τὰς τροφάς;
pass_a_gloss: Since teaching the disciples not to be rash (μὴ προπετεῖς) Jesus said to them: 'if they persecute (διώκωσιν) you in this city, flee (φεύγετε) to the other; and if in the other they persecute, again flee to another', and teaching became for them an example (παράδειγμα) of a steady (εὐσταθοῦς) life, one managing (οἰκονομοῦντος) not to go to close quarters (ὁμόσε χωρεῖν) with dangers at random (εἰκῆ) nor untimely (ἀκαίρως) and unreasonably (ἀλόγως): this again doing mischief (κακουργῶν) Celsus slanders (διαβάλλει), and the Jew in his work says to Jesus that 'with the disciples you run away (ἀποδιδράσκεις) here and there (τῇδε κἀκεῖσε)'. We shall say that like the slander (διαβολῇ) which he has made against Jesus and the disciples is also the thing recorded (ἱστορούμενον) about Aristotle; for he, seeing a court (δικαστήριον) about to be convened (συγκροτεῖσθαι) against him as against an impious man (ἀσεβοῦς) on account of certain doctrines (δόγματα) of his philosophy, which the Athenians thought to be impious, withdrawing (ἀναχωρήσας) from Athens held his lectures (διατριβάς) in Chalcis, defending himself (ἀπολογησάμενος) to his pupils (γνωρίμοις) and saying: 'let us depart from Athens, so that we may not give the Athenians a pretext (πρόφασιν) for taking up a second pollution/guilt (ἄγος) like that against Socrates, and so that they may not a second time commit impiety against philosophy'. And he says that Jesus with the disciples went about (περιεληλυθέναι) collecting (συλλέγοντα) food (τροφάς) shamefully (αἰσχρῶς) and meanly/beggarly (γλίσχρως). From where having got it, let him declare, the shameful and the beggarly of the collecting; for in the gospels 'certain women', 'healed from' their 'infirmities (ἀσθενειῶν)', among whom was also 'Susanna', provided (παρεῖχον) food to the disciples 'from their own possessions (ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς)'. And who of those philosophising and devoted (ἀνακειμένων) to the benefit (ὠφελίᾳ) of pupils did not take from them the things for needs (χρείας)? Or did those do this fittingly (καθηκόντως) and well, but whenever the disciples of Jesus do it, they are accused by Celsus as collecting food shamefully and beggarly?
pass_b_english: Jesus taught his disciples not to be rash, and said to them: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to the other; and if they persecute you in the other, flee again to another” (Matthew 10:23). And as he taught them, he became for them an example of a steady life, one that takes care not to go out to meet dangers at random, or at the wrong time, or without good reason. Here again Celsus maliciously misrepresents this, and his Jew says to Jesus: “With your disciples you run away, now here, now there.”

We shall say that the story told of Aristotle is just like what he slanders in Jesus and his disciples. For Aristotle saw that a court was about to be assembled against him as an impious man, because of certain doctrines of his philosophy which the Athenians thought impious. He withdrew from Athens and held his school at Chalcis, and he explained himself to his pupils, saying: “Let us leave Athens, so that we may not give the Athenians an occasion to bring on themselves a second guilt like their guilt over Socrates, and so that they may not commit impiety against philosophy a second time.”

He also says that Jesus “went about with his disciples collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way.” Let him tell us where he found the disgrace and the beggarliness in this collecting. For in the Gospels “certain women” who “had been healed of” their “infirmities,” among whom was “Susanna,” provided the disciples with food “out of their own means” (Luke 8:2–3). Which of those who practised philosophy and devoted themselves to the good of their pupils did not receive from them what they needed? Or did the philosophers do this fittingly and well, while the disciples of Jesus, when they do the same, are accused by Celsus of “collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way”?

choices.choice: Matthew 10:23 is quoted with the longer ending κἂν ἐν τῇ ἑτέρᾳ διώκωσι, πάλιν φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἄλλην ('and if they persecute you in the other, flee again to another'), a reading found in some witnesses of Matthew; Origen's form is kept. The Jew's words 'with your disciples you run away, now here, now there' are introduced by ὅτι but are in the second person, so they are set as a direct quotation. Aristotle's withdrawal to Chalcis and his saying are reported elsewhere in ancient sources, but Origen gives no source and the wording varies, so no inline source is given. 'Just like what he slanders in Jesus and his disciples' renders ὅμοιον... ᾗ πεποίηται... διαβολῇ: Aristotle's prudent withdrawal matches the conduct Celsus attacks. ἄγος is religious guilt or pollution; ἀσεβήσωσι is rendered 'commit impiety', not 'sin'. Luke 8:2–3 is quoted in fragments; Luke has 'healed of evil spirits and infirmities' and 'provided for them'; Origen says they provided food 'to the disciples'.
'This too' made 'Here again' (πάλιν was not rendered)
Aristotle comparison: 'is of a piece with the slander he has brought' made 'is just like what he slanders in', so the story is not itself called a slander
Aristotle's saying: 'a second crime' made 'a second guilt' (ἄγος); 'sin against philosophy' made 'commit impiety against philosophy' (ἀσεβήσωσι), a doctrinal-term fix
Celsus's charge: 'collecting his food' made 'collecting their food' (Jesus with the disciples, τὰς τροφάς)
Note updated to match; Matthew 10:23 and Luke 8:2-3 checked
